craft_claim: Staging the idea as a question-and-answer exchange lets the narrator externalise inquiry, so the reader watches a mind move instead of receiving a finished conclusion.

supporting_evidence.location: Cooper's introduction on the dialogue form; the Socratic dialogues generally
supporting_evidence.note: Confirms question-and-answer as Plato's chosen philosophical form: interlocutors' objections expose and test a claim in progress.

supporting_evidence.location: Chandogya Upanisad, the Uddalaka-Svetaketu teaching (esp. ch. 6)
supporting_evidence.note: The Upanisads teach abstract claims about self and reality through dialogue in which the student is led by questions, analogy and experiment to infer the principle.
The refrain structure and repeated questions model the reader's own approach to an abstract identity claim.

scope: Academic and blog explanation, philosophy-adjacent non-fiction, and fiction that carries an argument through dialogue.
exceptions: In forms that forbid character dialogue (some formal academic reports), the equivalent is a structured objection-and-response in the text itself.
